short_definition: The use of computers and software to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing patterns, or making decisions.
long_definition: Artificial intelligence is the broad field of building machines and software that can reason, learn, and act in ways that resemble human cognition. It covers a wide range of techniques, from simple rule-based systems built decades ago to today's large language models and generative AI tools. Not all AI is the same: some systems follow fixed rules (Traditional AI), while others learn patterns from data (Machine Learning). When people say 'AI' today, they usually mean the modern, data-driven kind.

short_definition: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data and improve their performance over time, instead of following rules that a person wrote out explicitly.
long_definition: Machine learning trains a model on examples (data) so it can make predictions or decisions on new, unseen inputs. Rather than programming every rule by hand, engineers feed the system data and let it find the patterns itself. ML underlies most modern AI capabilities, including recommendation engines, fraud detection, and the neural networks that power large language models. Deep Learning is the specific subset of ML that uses many-layered neural networks and drives most of today's generative AI.

short_definition: A type of machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks to find complex patterns in large amounts of data.
long_definition: Deep learning is what made the current wave of AI possible. By stacking many layers of artificial 'neurons,' a deep learning model can automatically discover intricate patterns in images, text, or audio without a person having to define what to look for. It's called 'deep' because of the number of layers involved (sometimes hundreds). Deep learning is the engine behind image recognition, speech-to-text, and large language models.

short_definition: A set of step-by-step instructions a computer follows to solve a problem or complete a task.
long_definition: An algorithm is the basic building block of any software, AI included: a defined sequence of steps for turning an input into an output, like a recipe. In AI, algorithms are what a model uses to learn from data (a 'learning algorithm') and what it uses to make decisions once trained. Not every algorithm involves AI or learning; a simple sorting function is an algorithm too. Understanding this distinction helps when a technical colleague says 'the algorithm' - they may mean anything from a basic rule to a full machine learning model.

short_definition: The field of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
long_definition: NLP is what lets a computer read a sentence and extract meaning from it, or generate a sentence that reads naturally. It covers tasks like translation, sentiment analysis, summarization, and the language understanding built into chatbots and virtual assistants. Large language models are the current state of the art in NLP, but the field predates them by decades and includes simpler techniques still used in production systems today (like keyword-based sentiment scoring).

short_definition: AI that creates new content - text, images, audio, video, or code - rather than just analyzing or classifying existing content.
long_definition: Generative AI models learn the patterns and structure of huge amounts of training data (books, images, code, etc.) and then use that knowledge to produce new, original outputs that resemble what they were trained on. This is the technology behind tools like ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Midjourney. It's a meaningful shift from 'traditional' AI, which was mostly built to classify, predict, or recommend rather than to create. For product teams, generative AI opens up entirely new categories of feature (drafting, summarizing, image creation) that weren't practical with older AI approaches.

short_definition: An AI model trained on massive amounts of text so it can understand and generate human-like language.
long_definition: LLMs are the technology behind tools like ChatGPT and Claude. They're built on a neural network architecture called a Transformer, trained on enormous text datasets (books, articles, code, web pages) to learn statistical relationships between words and concepts. Given a prompt, an LLM predicts the most likely next words, one at a time, which is how it produces coherent paragraphs, answers questions, or writes code. LLMs don't 'know' facts the way a database does - they generate plausible-sounding text based on patterns, which is why they can hallucinate (state incorrect things confidently).

short_definition: A hypothetical future AI that could perform any intellectual task a human can, across any domain, rather than being limited to specific tasks.
long_definition: AGI is a benchmark, not a product that exists today. Current AI systems (including the most advanced LLMs) are still considered 'narrow' - excellent at specific tasks but lacking the general, flexible reasoning and adaptability of a human. There's no universally agreed-upon definition or test for when AGI has been achieved, and different labs (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) define it somewhat differently. For PMs, AGI is useful mainly as a reference point in industry conversations about how close current models are to human-level general capability - it's more a topic of debate than an engineering spec.

short_definition: A computer program that simulates conversation with a human, usually through text or voice.
long_definition: Chatbots existed long before generative AI (early versions used simple scripted rules), but modern chatbots are typically powered by large language models, which let them hold much more natural, flexible conversations. A chatbot is really an application built on top of an LLM (or older NLP techniques) - the chatbot is the product surface, the LLM is what generates the responses underneath it.

short_definition: The trained system that takes an input and produces an output - the core 'thing' that has learned from data.
long_definition: In everyday conversation, 'model' is often used loosely to mean 'the AI,' but more precisely, a model is the mathematical structure (millions or billions of learned parameters) that resulted from training on data. GPT-5.6, Claude, and Gemini are all examples of specific models. A single product (like ChatGPT) can switch between different underlying models over time. Knowing this distinction helps when engineers talk about 'swapping the model' or 'the model version' - they're talking about the underlying system, not the product interface.

short_definition: AI software that can autonomously plan and take multi-step actions to reach a goal, rather than just answering a single question.
long_definition: An AI agent goes beyond a single prompt-and-response interaction: it can break a task into steps, decide which tools or systems to use (web search, code execution, other apps), take action, evaluate the result, and adjust its plan - often with limited human supervision in between steps. 'Agentic AI' is the broader category/architecture describing this style of system. This is a fast-moving, still-maturing space; infrastructure and best practices for building reliable agents are still being worked out industry-wide, so expect the term's practical meaning to keep sharpening.

short_definition: The input - a question, instruction, or piece of text - that a person gives an AI model to get a response.
long_definition: A prompt can be as simple as a one-line question or as elaborate as a detailed set of instructions, examples, and context. Because generative AI models respond directly to what's in the prompt, the way a prompt is worded has a real effect on the quality and relevance of the output - which is the whole premise behind Prompt Engineering.

short_definition: The practice of crafting and refining prompts to get better, more reliable outputs from an AI model.
long_definition: Prompt engineering includes techniques like giving the model examples of the output you want (few-shot prompting), asking it to reason step by step (chain of thought), specifying a role or format, or adding constraints. It's become a practical skill for PMs and other non-engineers because it doesn't require touching the model itself - just being deliberate about how you ask. As models improve, some prompt-engineering tricks matter less over time, but the underlying discipline of being clear about what you want remains useful.

short_definition: The amount of text (measured in tokens) an AI model can 'see' and consider at one time when generating a response.
long_definition: Think of the context window as the model's working memory for a single conversation or task - it's different from the vast training data the model learned from originally. If a conversation or document exceeds the context window, the model starts losing track of earlier information. Context windows have grown enormously (some current models handle over a million tokens - roughly hundreds of pages of text), which is what enables use cases like uploading a large document and asking detailed questions about it.

short_definition: When an AI model generates information that sounds plausible and confident but is factually incorrect or entirely made up.
long_definition: Hallucinations happen because generative models are built to produce statistically likely text, not to verify facts against a source of truth. A model might invent a citation, misstate a date, or confidently describe an event that never happened. This is one of the most important limitations for PMs to understand and design around - especially in any product surface where users might treat AI output as authoritative. Techniques like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and grounding are common mitigations.

short_definition: When an AI system produces outputs that unfairly favor or disadvantage certain groups or perspectives, usually as a result of patterns in its training data.
long_definition: Bias can creep in from skewed or unrepresentative training data, from the way a problem is framed, or from limitations in the model itself. It can show up subtly (an image generator underrepresenting certain groups) or more seriously (a hiring or lending tool producing discriminatory outcomes). Addressing bias is an active area of AI Ethics and Responsible AI practice, and it's a live risk consideration for any product that puts AI output in front of real users or decisions.

short_definition: Taking an already-trained AI model and training it further on a smaller, specific dataset so it performs better on a particular task or domain.
long_definition: Fine-tuning lets a company adapt a general-purpose model (like a foundation model) to their own use case - for example, training it on customer support transcripts so it responds more like a company's support team, or on legal documents so it uses domain-appropriate language. It's cheaper and faster than training a model from scratch, since the model already has broad language understanding baked in. Fine-tuning is different from Prompt Engineering: prompt engineering changes what you ask at the moment of use, while fine-tuning changes the model itself ahead of time.

short_definition: The data used to teach an AI model - the examples it learns patterns from during training.
long_definition: Training data quality and diversity directly determine what a model can and can't do well, and where its biases and blind spots come from. For an LLM, training data typically means enormous volumes of text scraped from books, websites, and other sources; for a fine-tuned model, it might mean a much smaller, curated set of company-specific examples. See also Dataset - training data is a dataset that's specifically being used to train a model, though the two terms are sometimes used interchangeably in casual conversation.

short_definition: A structured collection of data - which may or may not be used to train an AI model.
long_definition: A dataset is the broader concept: any organized collection of information, such as a spreadsheet of customer transactions or a folder of labeled images. Training Data is a dataset that's specifically being used to teach a model. In practice the terms overlap a lot and are often used interchangeably, but it's worth knowing that not every dataset is training data - a dataset might instead be used for testing, validation, or plain old analytics with no AI involved at all.

short_definition: The small chunks of text (words, parts of words, or characters) that an AI language model breaks input into before processing it.
long_definition: Tokenization is the process of splitting text into these units. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word in English, on average. Tokens matter for two practical reasons: they determine how much text fits in a model's context window, and most AI providers charge based on the number of tokens processed, so token count is directly tied to cost.

short_definition: A technique that lets an AI model look up relevant information from an external source before generating its answer, instead of relying only on what it learned during training.
long_definition: RAG addresses two big LLM limitations: models can't access information created after their training cutoff, and they sometimes hallucinate facts. With RAG, a query first retrieves relevant documents (from a company's knowledge base, a set of PDFs, or the live web), and that retrieved content is added to the prompt so the model can ground its answer in real source material - often with citations. This is one of the most common patterns for building reliable, up-to-date AI product features, especially ones that draw on proprietary or frequently-changing information.

short_definition: A training method where an AI system learns by taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties based on the outcome, gradually improving its behavior through trial and error.
long_definition: Reinforcement learning is how systems learn to play games, control robots, and - critically for today's chatbots - refine their responses based on feedback about what a 'good' answer looks like. It's fundamentally different from supervised learning: instead of being shown labeled correct answers, the system explores, gets feedback, and adjusts.

short_definition: A machine learning approach where a model is trained on data that's already labeled with the correct answer, so it learns to map inputs to outputs.
long_definition: This is one of the two classic machine learning paradigms (the other being unsupervised learning). Supervised learning is used for tasks like classification (is this email spam?) or prediction (what will this house sell for?), where you have historical examples paired with known correct outcomes. It requires labeled data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to produce - a practical constraint worth knowing when scoping any ML feature.

short_definition: A machine learning approach where a model finds patterns or groupings in data on its own, without being given labeled correct answers.
long_definition: Because there's no 'right answer' provided during training, unsupervised learning is used to discover structure that wasn't obvious beforehand - like clustering customers into segments based on behavior, or reducing a complex dataset down to its most important variables. It's especially useful when labeled data is scarce or expensive to produce, which is common in real-world business data.

short_definition: AI designed to perform one specific task or a limited set of tasks well, without the ability to generalize beyond that scope.
long_definition: Essentially all AI in production use today - including the most advanced chatbots - is narrow AI. A narrow AI system can be extraordinarily capable within its lane (translating language, generating images, playing chess) but can't transfer that skill to unrelated problems the way a human can. This is the practical contrast point to AGI, which remains hypothetical.

short_definition: A large-scale AI model trained on broad, diverse data, designed to be adapted (via fine-tuning or prompting) for many different downstream tasks.
long_definition: Foundation models are the 'base layer' companies build on rather than training a model from scratch - think of GPT, Claude, or Gemini's underlying models. The term is broader than 'LLM': a foundation model can be multimodal (handling text, images, audio) whereas 'LLM' technically refers to the text-focused case. Most generative AI products today are built by prompting or fine-tuning an existing foundation model rather than training something new.

short_definition: AI systems that can understand and generate more than one type of content - such as text, images, audio, and video - within the same interaction.
long_definition: Multimodal AI is what lets you upload a photo and ask a chatbot to describe it, or ask a model to generate an image from a text description. It reflects models moving beyond text-only understanding toward something closer to how humans naturally combine senses and modes of communication. This capability is increasingly table-stakes in major consumer AI products.

short_definition: Using technology, including but not limited to AI, to perform tasks based on fixed, predefined rules with little or no human involvement.
long_definition: It's useful to distinguish automation from AI agents: automation follows rules a person explicitly defined ('if X happens, do Y'), while an AI agent can interpret a goal and figure out its own steps to get there. Plenty of valuable automation involves no AI or machine learning at all - it's worth not over-attributing every automated workflow to 'AI.'

short_definition: A field of AI focused on enabling computers to interpret and understand visual information from images and video.
long_definition: Computer vision powers things like facial recognition, medical image analysis, object detection in self-driving cars, and the 'describe this photo' capability in multimodal chatbots. It's one of the older, more established branches of AI, predating the current generative AI wave by decades, though it's been transformed by deep learning.

short_definition: A security attack where malicious instructions are hidden in text (a webpage, document, or message) to trick an AI model into ignoring its original instructions and doing something unintended.
long_definition: As AI agents increasingly browse the web, read documents, or process untrusted content, prompt injection becomes a real product-security risk - not just an academic curiosity. For example, hidden text on a webpage could instruct an AI agent to leak confidential data or take an unauthorized action. This is a risk category PMs should know exists, even without needing to understand the technical mitigations in depth.

short_definition: A technique (and model behavior) where an AI works through a problem step by step, showing its intermediate reasoning, rather than jumping straight to a final answer.
long_definition: Just as a person might use scratch paper to work through a math problem instead of guessing the answer outright, chain-of-thought prompting/reasoning breaks a problem into smaller steps. This tends to improve accuracy on logic, math, and multi-step problems, though it takes the model longer to respond. 'Reasoning Models' are a newer category of models specifically built and trained to do this kind of step-by-step thinking well.

short_definition: Hidden instructions given to an AI model before a conversation starts, which set its behavior, tone, or boundaries without the end user seeing them.
long_definition: A system prompt might tell a model 'You are a helpful customer support assistant for Acme Co. Don't discuss competitor products.' It's how companies customize an off-the-shelf model's behavior for their product without fine-tuning it. Understanding system prompts matters for PMs designing AI features, since much of a product's AI 'personality' and guardrails often live here rather than in the underlying model itself.

short_definition: A setting that controls how random or creative an AI model's output is - lower values produce more predictable, focused answers; higher values produce more varied, surprising ones.
long_definition: Temperature is a dial product teams can adjust depending on the use case: a customer support bot might use a low temperature for consistent, safe answers, while a creative writing tool might use a higher temperature to encourage variety. It's one of the few AI model settings that's genuinely simple to explain to a non-technical stakeholder.

short_definition: Rules, filters, and safeguards put in place around an AI system to prevent it from producing harmful, inappropriate, or off-brand content.
long_definition: Guardrails can be built at multiple layers: in the system prompt, through content filtering on inputs and outputs, or through separate moderation models that check responses before they reach the user. Every product shipping an AI feature to real users needs to think about guardrails - both for safety/legal reasons and for maintaining product quality and brand voice.

short_definition: AI system design where a human reviews, approves, or can override the AI's output at some point in the process, rather than letting the AI act fully autonomously.
long_definition: Human-in-the-loop is a common and often necessary design pattern for higher-stakes AI features - for example, having a person approve an AI-drafted email before it sends, or review an AI's content moderation decision before it's enforced. It's a key lever PMs have for managing risk and building trust while still capturing much of the efficiency benefit of AI.

short_definition: The process of a trained AI model actually generating an output (a prediction, an answer, an image) in response to new input.
long_definition: Training is the (usually one-time, expensive) process of teaching a model; inference is what happens every single time someone uses the model afterward. This distinction matters commercially: most of the ongoing cost of running an AI product comes from inference (serving responses to users), not from the original training.

short_definition: An AI model's ability to correctly perform a task or recognize something it was never explicitly trained or shown examples of.
long_definition: Modern LLMs can often follow a brand-new instruction correctly on the first try, without needing any examples in the prompt - that's zero-shot performance. Contrast this with Few-Shot Learning, where you give the model a handful of examples in the prompt to guide its response, which often improves accuracy on more specific or unusual tasks.

short_definition: The time delay between sending a prompt to an AI model and receiving its response.
long_definition: Latency is a practical product concern: a slower model may give better answers but hurt the user experience in real-time contexts like chat. Two sub-metrics matter in technical conversations - Time to First Token (how fast the response starts appearing) and total response time (how long the full answer takes) - and they can be optimized somewhat independently.

short_definition: AI models whose underlying code, and often trained weights, are made publicly available for anyone to use, inspect, or modify.
long_definition: Open-source and open-weight models (like Meta's Llama family) let companies run AI on their own infrastructure, customize it more deeply, and avoid depending entirely on a single vendor's API - trade-offs against the convenience and cutting-edge performance of closed, proprietary models like GPT or Claude. This build-vs-buy-style decision is a real strategic question for AI product teams.

short_definition: The tendency to attribute human traits, emotions, or intentions to AI systems that don't actually have them.
long_definition: Because chatbots can hold fluent, natural-sounding conversations, people often unconsciously treat them as if they have feelings, opinions, or consciousness - even though today's AI has none of these things. This matters for product design: anthropomorphism can create unrealistic user expectations and even unhealthy emotional attachment, but thoughtfully designed personality can also make interactions feel more natural and approachable. It's a genuine design trade-off, not just a curiosity.

short_definition: Connecting an AI model's output to verifiable, real source material - like documents, databases, or search results - to make its answers more accurate and trustworthy.
long_definition: Grounding is the general concept; Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the most common technique used to achieve it. A grounded response can often cite exactly where its information came from, which reduces (though doesn't eliminate) the risk of hallucination.

short_definition: A way of converting text, images, or other data into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so a computer can compare how similar two pieces of content are.
long_definition: Embeddings turn the fuzzy, human idea of 'similar meaning' into something a computer can calculate mathematically - two pieces of text about the same topic end up numerically 'close' to each other even if they don't share the same words. This is the technology underneath semantic search, recommendation systems, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation, where a system needs to find the most relevant piece of stored information for a given query.

short_definition: A specialized database designed to store and quickly search through embeddings - the numerical representations of text, images, or other data.
long_definition: Traditional databases are built to search for exact matches or filter by fields; vector databases are built to answer 'what's most similar to this?' - which is exactly what's needed for semantic search and RAG systems. If a PM hears an engineer mention Pinecone, Weaviate, or pgvector, they're talking about vector database technology.

short_definition: An open standard that lets AI models connect to external tools and data sources - like files, databases, or apps - in a consistent way, without a custom integration for every pairing.
long_definition: MCP was introduced by Anthropic and has since been adopted industry-wide (including by OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft), making it one of the fastest-spreading standards in recent AI history. It's often described as a 'USB-C port for AI' - a common connector instead of a different plug for every device. For PMs, MCP is relevant because it's rapidly becoming the default way AI agents plug into a company's existing tools and data.

short_definition: The neural network architecture, introduced in 2017, that underlies nearly all modern large language models.
long_definition: Transformers process an entire sequence of text at once (using a mechanism called 'attention' to weigh how relevant every word is to every other word), rather than reading word-by-word in order. This made it possible to train much larger, more capable language models than earlier architectures allowed, and it's the single biggest technical breakthrough behind the current generative AI wave.

short_definition: A family of large language models, originally developed by OpenAI, built on the Transformer architecture and trained to generate human-like text.
long_definition: GPT is both a general architecture/training approach and, informally, shorthand for OpenAI's specific model line (which now includes many versions). It's worth knowing 'GPT' as a category name distinct from 'ChatGPT' (the product) - GPT is the underlying model technology, ChatGPT is the consumer chat product built on top of it.

short_definition: A training technique that uses human rankings of AI outputs to teach a model to produce responses people prefer.
long_definition: After initial training, human reviewers compare pairs of model outputs and indicate which is better; the model is then further trained to favor outputs like the ones humans preferred. This is a major reason today's chatbots feel helpful and conversational rather than just technically fluent - RLHF is what's typically used to align a raw language model with being a genuinely useful assistant.

short_definition: A technique where a model trained on one task is reused as the starting point for a different, related task, instead of training a new model from scratch.
long_definition: Transfer learning is the general principle that makes fine-tuning practical: a foundation model already 'knows' a lot about language, so adapting it to a specific task requires far less additional data and compute than starting over. It's especially valuable when you don't have much data for your specific use case, since the model brings broad prior knowledge with it.

short_definition: The initial, large-scale training phase where a model learns general language patterns from a massive, broad dataset, before any task-specific fine-tuning happens.
long_definition: A pretrained model has learned to predict likely text based on everything it's seen, but it isn't naturally good at following instructions or answering questions helpfully on its own - that behavior typically comes from further steps like fine-tuning and RLHF. When people talk about 'the base model' versus 'the assistant,' pretraining is what produced the base model.

short_definition: A newer category of AI models specifically trained to work through complex problems step by step before producing a final answer, improving accuracy on logic, math, and multi-step tasks.
long_definition: Reasoning models are built from standard LLMs but further trained (often with reinforcement learning) to reliably do chain-of-thought-style thinking, rather than just sometimes doing it when prompted. They tend to be slower and more expensive per response than standard models, since they're doing more internal 'thinking' before answering - a real cost/latency trade-off for product teams to weigh against the accuracy gains.

short_definition: The internal numerical values within an AI model that are adjusted during training and ultimately determine how it behaves.
long_definition: A model's parameter count (often described in the billions) is a rough, imperfect proxy for its scale and capability - more parameters generally mean more capacity to capture complex patterns, though it's far from the whole story. When you hear a model described as having '70 billion parameters,' this is what's being referenced.

short_definition: A type of generative AI model made of two competing neural networks - a generator that creates content and a discriminator that tries to tell real from fake - that improve each other through competition.
long_definition: GANs were one of the earliest breakthroughs in generating realistic synthetic images, and remain in use for certain image and data-synthesis tasks, though diffusion models have become the dominant approach for most modern image generation (like DALL-E and Midjourney).

short_definition: A type of generative AI model that creates content (typically images) by starting with random noise and gradually refining it into a coherent output.
long_definition: Diffusion models are trained to reverse a process of adding random 'noise' to an image until it's unrecognizable, which teaches them how to do the opposite: start from noise and progressively sharpen it into a realistic image. This is the core technology behind most modern image generators, including DALL-E and Midjourney.

short_definition: A specialized computer chip, originally built for rendering video game graphics, that's also extremely efficient at the mathematical calculations AI training and inference require.
long_definition: GPUs can perform many calculations simultaneously (in parallel), which is exactly what training and running neural networks demands. GPU availability and cost are a real, ongoing bottleneck and cost driver across the AI industry - worth understanding at a basic level when discussing AI infrastructure costs or scaling plans.

short_definition: Shorthand for the computational resources (processing power, typically GPUs or TPUs) needed to train or run an AI model.
long_definition: 'Compute' is used constantly in AI industry conversations as a stand-in for cost and capacity - training a large model requires enormous amounts of compute, and running inference at scale for millions of users requires ongoing compute capacity too. Understanding compute as a cost driver helps PMs reason about the economics of any AI feature, especially ones with high usage volume.

short_definition: When a deployed AI model's performance degrades over time because real-world data has changed since the model was trained.
long_definition: A model trained on last year's customer behavior might perform worse today if customer patterns have shifted. This is an important operational concept for PMs: shipping an AI feature isn't a one-time launch - it requires ongoing monitoring to catch drift and a plan (retraining, fine-tuning, or replacing the model) for when performance degrades.

short_definition: Artificially generated data, created by an algorithm or model, used in place of or alongside real-world data - often to train other AI models.
long_definition: Synthetic data is useful when real data is scarce, expensive, sensitive (like medical or financial records), or imbalanced in ways that would bias a model. It's an increasingly important part of training-data strategy, though it carries its own risk: a model trained too heavily on synthetic data can inherit and amplify the flaws of whatever generated that data.

short_definition: Methods and techniques designed to make an AI system's decisions understandable to humans, rather than functioning as an unexplainable 'black box.'
long_definition: XAI matters most in high-stakes settings - healthcare, lending, hiring, legal - where regulators, users, or internal stakeholders need to understand why a model made a particular decision, not just what the decision was. It's closely related to but distinct from Interpretability, which refers to the underlying degree of transparency a model has; XAI is the set of techniques used to achieve or improve that transparency.

short_definition: Making sure an AI system's goals and behavior actually match what people want - its creators' intentions and broader human values.
long_definition: Alignment is a central concern in both practical product terms (does this chatbot behave the way our brand and users need it to?) and in longer-term AI safety research (as AI systems become more autonomous and capable, will their objectives stay compatible with human interests?). RLHF is one of the most common practical techniques used to align a model's behavior with human preferences.

short_definition: The field focused on ensuring AI systems behave reliably and don't cause harm, even as they become more powerful or are deployed in unexpected situations.
long_definition: AI safety spans a spectrum from near-term, practical concerns (a chatbot giving dangerous advice, an agent taking an unintended harmful action) to longer-term, more speculative questions about very advanced future AI systems. For product teams, the near-term end of this spectrum is directly relevant to risk assessment and guardrail design.

short_definition: The principles and practices guiding the responsible development and use of AI, covering issues like fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability.
long_definition: AI ethics is the umbrella under which more specific concerns - bias, fairness, explainability, data privacy - all sit. It's increasingly not just a philosophical topic but a practical, sometimes regulatory, requirement for any company shipping AI-powered products.

short_definition: The practical frameworks and processes companies use to develop and deploy AI in a way that's ethical, safe, and accountable.
long_definition: Where 'AI Ethics' describes the principles, 'Responsible AI' usually refers to the operational practice of applying them - things like bias testing before launch, clear escalation paths when an AI feature misbehaves, and documentation of how a model was trained and evaluated. Many companies now have formal Responsible AI review processes that PMs shipping AI features need to go through.

short_definition: A modeling problem where an AI model learns the training data too closely - including its noise and quirks - and performs poorly on new, unseen data as a result.
long_definition: An overfit model looks great on the data it was trained and tested on, but fails to generalize to real-world use, which is the entire point of building it. It's a bit like a student who memorizes the exact answers to practice questions instead of understanding the underlying material, then struggles when the real exam asks something slightly different. This is a core quality-control concept in any ML evaluation process.

short_definition: OpenAI's consumer AI chatbot product, launched in November 2022, built on their GPT family of language models.
long_definition: ChatGPT is widely credited with bringing generative AI into mainstream awareness and use. It's a product (the chat interface and app), distinct from GPT (the underlying model family) - OpenAI has swapped and upgraded the model powering ChatGPT many times since launch.

short_definition: OpenAI's AI image-generation model/product, which creates images from text descriptions.
long_definition: DALL-E was one of the earliest widely-used text-to-image tools and helped popularize generative image AI alongside Midjourney. It has since been through multiple versions and, as of 2026, has largely been superseded within ChatGPT by OpenAI's newer image models.

short_definition: An independent AI image-generation product, accessed primarily through Discord, known for highly stylized, artistic image outputs.
long_definition: Midjourney is one of the most widely recognized names in AI image generation, often noted for a distinctive aesthetic quality that made it popular with designers and artists specifically (as opposed to DALL-E's more general-purpose positioning).

short_definition: Anthropic's family of AI assistant models and chat product.
long_definition: Claude is a major LLM-based assistant, comparable in category to ChatGPT and Gemini, developed by Anthropic with a particular emphasis on safety and helpfulness research (see HHH).

short_definition: Google's family of multimodal AI models and assistant product, integrated across Google's products including Search.
long_definition: Gemini is Google's flagship LLM/assistant line, positioned as a direct competitor to ChatGPT and Claude, and increasingly embedded into Google Search results (AI Overviews) and other Google products.

short_definition: Microsoft's AI assistant, built on OpenAI's models and integrated across Microsoft products like Windows, Office, and GitHub.
long_definition: Copilot is Microsoft's branding for AI assistance across its ecosystem - notably including GitHub Copilot, a widely used AI coding assistant, which is a distinct product under the same brand umbrella.

short_definition: Meta's family of open-weight large language models.
long_definition: Llama is one of the most prominent open-weight model families, meaning its trained weights are publicly available for others to download, run, and build on - a meaningfully different distribution model than the closed, API-only approach of GPT or Claude.

short_definition: An AI-powered answer engine that combines a language model with live web search to produce cited, sourced answers.
long_definition: Perplexity is a well-known example of a product built around Retrieval-Augmented Generation and grounding - its core value proposition is answering questions with citations rather than functioning as a general-purpose chatbot.

short_definition: OpenAI's AI video-generation model/product, which creates video clips from text descriptions.
long_definition: Sora represents generative AI's extension into video, following the earlier progression from text to image generation. It's included here as a notable product despite being a single company's offering, since video generation is a distinct enough capability category worth PMs recognizing by name.

short_definition: A computing structure loosely inspired by the brain, made of layered nodes that learn to recognize patterns in data.
long_definition: Neural networks are the foundational architecture behind deep learning. Each layer of interconnected 'neurons' processes the data it receives and passes a transformed version to the next layer, allowing the network to gradually build up an understanding of complex patterns - from edges and shapes in an image to grammar and meaning in text. Modern variants like Convolutional Neural Networks (for images) and Transformers (for language) are specialized architectures built on this same basic idea. NOTE: this term was accidentally omitted from the priority-1 batch - included here as a make-up entry.

short_definition: The process of teaching an AI model by having it learn patterns from a dataset.
long_definition: Training is the (often expensive, one-time) phase where a model's parameters are adjusted based on exposure to data, as opposed to Inference, which is what happens every time the trained model is actually used afterward. Training can refer to a model's original, large-scale pretraining or to a later fine-tuning step. NOTE: also omitted from the priority-2 batch - included here as a make-up entry.

short_definition: A hypothetical AI that would surpass human intelligence across every domain, beyond even AGI.
long_definition: ASI is a speculative concept describing AI that doesn't just match human-level general intelligence (AGI) but dramatically exceeds it. No such system exists today, and there's active debate about whether or how it could emerge. For product teams, ASI is mostly relevant as a term you'll hear in industry-wide policy and safety conversations, not as something with practical product implications today.

short_definition: AI agents specialized for writing, testing, and debugging software code with minimal human intervention.
long_definition: Coding agents extend the general AI agent concept to software development specifically - they can work across an entire codebase, run tests, and push fixes autonomously, rather than just suggesting a snippet for a developer to review. Tools built into GitHub Copilot's agent mode are examples. They still typically require human review before changes ship.

short_definition: A classic test, proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, for whether a machine's conversation is indistinguishable from a human's.
long_definition: In the test, a human judge exchanges typed messages with both a human and a machine, without knowing which is which; if the judge can't reliably tell them apart, the machine is said to have passed. The Turing Test predates modern AI by decades and is now considered a limited measure of intelligence - a system can pass it through clever mimicry without genuine understanding - but it remains a foundational reference point in conversations about what 'intelligent' AI means.

short_definition: Older AI approaches based on explicitly programmed rules and logic, rather than learning patterns from data.
long_definition: Traditional AI (sometimes called symbolic or rule-based AI) was the dominant approach for decades before machine learning became practical at scale - a human expert would encode 'if this, then that' logic directly into the system. It's a useful contrast point for explaining why today's generative AI, which learns from data instead of fixed rules, behaves so differently, including why it can be creative and flexible, but also why it can hallucinate.

short_definition: The field combining engineering, computer science, and increasingly AI to build machines that can perform physical tasks.
long_definition: AI has become an increasingly important component of modern robotics, giving robots the ability to perceive their environment, plan actions, and adapt to changing conditions rather than just following fixed physical motions. Applications span manufacturing, warehouse automation, self-driving vehicles, and consumer devices.

short_definition: Early AI programs that mimicked a human expert's decision-making using a fixed set of rules and facts about a specific domain.
long_definition: Expert systems were among the first commercially successful AI applications, widely used in fields like medical diagnosis and financial approval decisions well before machine learning became practical. They work by applying if-then logic to a hand-built knowledge base, rather than learning patterns from data - reliable and explainable, but rigid and expensive to maintain as rules multiply. A useful historical reference point for how AI approaches have evolved.

short_definition: Feeding the output of one AI prompt as the input to a following prompt, creating a sequence of steps that build on each other.
long_definition: Rather than trying to get a complex task done in a single prompt, prompt chaining breaks it into smaller steps - for example, first asking a model to outline a document, then asking it to draft each section based on that outline. This is a common pattern behind more sophisticated AI agent workflows, where each step's output informs the next.

short_definition: Giving an AI model a handful of examples within the prompt to help it understand exactly the kind of output you want.
long_definition: Few-shot learning sits between zero-shot (no examples at all) and full fine-tuning (retraining the model on many examples). By showing the model 2-5 examples of the input/output pattern you want, you can often significantly improve accuracy on unusual or highly specific tasks without any additional training.

short_definition: The internal numerical values a neural network adjusts during training that determine how strongly different inputs influence its output.
long_definition: Weights are what actually gets 'learned' during training - conceptually, they're the model's accumulated knowledge, encoded as numbers rather than anything a human could read directly. When people discuss a model's 'weights' being open or closed, they're talking about whether this underlying, trained knowledge is published for others to download and run.

short_definition: Software (or AI models) whose underlying code and/or weights are kept private and not available for others to inspect or modify.
long_definition: Closed-source AI, like OpenAI's GPT models, is typically accessed only through an API or product interface - you can use it, but not see or change how it works internally. This is the contrast case to Open Source and Open-Weight models; the choice between them is a real strategic consideration, since closed models often offer more cutting-edge performance and less operational overhead, while open ones offer more control and independence.

short_definition: An AI model whose trained parameters (weights) are published publicly, so anyone can download and run it themselves.
long_definition: Open-weight models (like Meta's Llama family) differ from fully open-source models in a subtle but important way: the trained weights are available, but the original training code and data might not be. This still lets companies run the model on their own infrastructure and avoid being locked into a single vendor's API - a meaningfully different distribution and control trade-off than closed models like GPT or Claude.

short_definition: An AI model's tendency to agree with or flatter the user, even when the user's reasoning is flawed.
long_definition: Because many models are trained (via RLHF) partly on human preference ratings, they can learn to optimize for what people rate highly in the moment - which sometimes means telling users what they want to hear rather than what's accurate. This is a real product-quality and trust concern: a sycophantic assistant might validate a bad decision instead of offering honest pushback.

short_definition: Writing software by describing what you want in plain language to an AI coding assistant, rather than writing code by hand line by line.
long_definition: Vibe coding has become a popular term for a genuinely new workflow: a person (technical or not) describes a desired outcome conversationally, and an AI agent generates, tests, and iterates on the actual code. It's lowered the barrier to building simple software prototypes considerably, though it still generally benefits from technical review before anything goes to production.

short_definition: A structured way of representing information as a network of entities (people, places, concepts) and the relationships between them.
long_definition: Knowledge graphs let a system answer questions that depend on connections between facts, not just a single fact in isolation - Google's Knowledge Graph, for example, powers many info boxes that appear directly in search results. In AI systems, knowledge graphs are often used alongside or as an alternative to embeddings/vector search for representing and reasoning over structured knowledge.

short_definition: A capability that lets an AI model request that a specific external tool or piece of code be run on its behalf, then use the result in its response.
long_definition: Function calling is what allows a language model to go beyond generating text and actually take action - calling a weather API, querying a database, or triggering a workflow. It's a core building block of AI agents: the model decides which function to call and what inputs to pass, and the surrounding application executes it and returns the result.

short_definition: A technique that lets a neural network figure out which parts of the input are most relevant to each other when producing an output.
long_definition: Attention is the key innovation behind the Transformer architecture: instead of processing a sentence strictly in order, an attention mechanism lets the model weigh how much every word should influence the interpretation of every other word, even across long distances in the text. This is a big part of why transformer-based LLMs are so much better at understanding context than earlier architectures.

short_definition: An early, influential language model developed by Google that helped models understand word meaning based on surrounding context.
long_definition: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) was a major NLP milestone, reading text in both directions at once to better capture context and nuance than earlier models. It's mostly used today as a component within other systems (like search ranking) rather than as a consumer-facing chatbot, but it's historically significant and still referenced often in technical AI discussions.

short_definition: A training method where a model creates its own learning signal from raw, unlabeled data, rather than needing humans to label it.
long_definition: Self-supervised learning is how most large language models are pretrained: the model is given a task like 'predict the next word' using ordinary text, so no manual labeling is required at all. This is a major reason LLMs could be trained on such enormous amounts of internet text - there was no need to have humans label any of it first.

short_definition: A form of fine-tuning where a model is trained specifically to follow instructions and complete tasks as directed, rather than just predicting likely next words.
long_definition: A raw, pretrained language model is good at continuing text plausibly, but not necessarily good at following an explicit instruction like 'summarize this in three bullet points.' Instruction tuning closes that gap by training the model on many examples of instructions paired with the desired response, which is a key step (alongside RLHF) in turning a base model into a genuinely useful assistant.

short_definition: A technique for creating a smaller, faster AI model that mimics the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model.
long_definition: In distillation, a large, expensive-to-run model generates outputs, and a smaller 'student' model is trained to reproduce those outputs as closely as possible. The result is a lighter, cheaper model that approximates the larger one's behavior - useful when you need to deploy AI at scale or on limited hardware without matching the full cost of the original model.

short_definition: Reducing the numerical precision of a model's internal values to make it smaller and faster to run, at some cost to accuracy.
long_definition: Quantization is a bit like compressing an image: a 16-megapixel photo and an 8-megapixel version of the same photo both look clear at a glance, but the higher-resolution one holds more detail on close inspection. Quantized models take up less memory and run faster/cheaper, in exchange for a modest hit to output quality.

short_definition: A model architecture that splits a large neural network into many smaller specialized sub-networks, activating only a few of them for any given task.
long_definition: Rather than routing every request through an entire massive model, an MoE model has a 'router' that picks just the most relevant specialist sub-networks to handle each specific input. This lets a model be enormous in total size while staying relatively fast and cheap to run, since only a fraction of it is doing work at any one time.

short_definition: A setting configured before training begins that controls how a model learns, as opposed to the parameters the model learns on its own.
long_definition: Hyperparameters are choices a human (or an automated search process) makes ahead of time, like how fast the model should adjust during training or how many layers a neural network should have. Tuning these settings well can meaningfully affect a model's final performance, and is a distinct step from the training process itself.

short_definition: A mathematical formula that measures how wrong a model's predictions are, which the training process tries to minimize.
long_definition: During training, a model makes a prediction, the loss function scores how far off that prediction was from the correct answer, and the model adjusts its internal weights to reduce that score next time. Choosing the right loss function for a given task is a key design decision in building any machine learning system, closely related to the broader idea of an Objective Function.

short_definition: The algorithm neural networks use to learn from their mistakes, by tracing an error back through the network to figure out which internal values to adjust.
long_definition: After a neural network makes a prediction and the loss function scores how wrong it was, backpropagation calculates how much each individual weight in the network contributed to that error, working backward from the output layer to the input layer. This is the core mechanism that makes deep learning trainable at all.

short_definition: When a model is too simple to capture the real patterns in the data, performing poorly on both training data and new data.
long_definition: Underfitting is the opposite failure mode from overfitting: instead of memorizing the training data too closely, an underfit model hasn't learned enough from it in the first place - often because it's too simple, under-trained, or lacking enough relevant data. Both failure modes result in a model that doesn't generalize well to real-world use.

short_definition: A neural network architecture specifically designed to process grid-like data, most commonly images.
long_definition: CNNs use layers of filters that scan across an image to detect increasingly complex visual features - starting with simple edges and textures, building up to recognizing whole objects. They were the dominant architecture for computer vision tasks for years and remain foundational to modern image-processing systems like medical imaging and facial recognition.

short_definition: A neural network architecture designed to process sequences of data, where each step's output feeds into the next.
long_definition: RNNs were the standard approach for sequential data - text, speech, time-series - before Transformers took over, since they process one element at a time while retaining some memory of what came before. They struggled with very long sequences, a limitation that specialized variants like LSTM partially addressed and that Transformers ultimately solved more effectively.

short_definition: A compressed, mathematical representation of data where similar things end up positioned close together.
long_definition: When a model processes complex data like images or text, it often first compresses it into a simplified numerical form that captures the essential features while discarding noise - this compressed representation is the latent space. It's a core concept behind embeddings, image generation, and how models discover that concepts like 'king' and 'queen' are related without ever being told so explicitly.

short_definition: Artificially expanding a training dataset by creating modified versions of existing examples, rather than collecting entirely new data.
long_definition: For example, a dataset of product photos might be augmented by rotating, cropping, or adjusting the lighting of existing images to create new training examples without needing to photograph more products. This helps models generalize better and reduces overfitting, especially when collecting more real-world data is expensive or slow.

short_definition: Using historical data and statistical methods to forecast future outcomes or trends.
long_definition: Predictive analytics predates the current AI boom and includes techniques from classical statistics as well as modern machine learning. It's used across business functions like demand forecasting, churn prediction, and risk scoring. Predictive AI is the newer, AI-specific framing of this same general idea.

short_definition: Using AI to determine the emotional tone (positive, negative, neutral) expressed in a piece of text.
long_definition: Sentiment analysis is a common, practical NLP application - used for things like scoring customer reviews, monitoring social media reaction to a launch, or flagging frustrated customer support messages for escalation. It's often one of the more straightforward, well-established AI capabilities a product team might build or buy.

short_definition: Predictable relationships showing how an AI model's performance tends to improve as its size, training data, and compute increase.
long_definition: Scaling laws are part of why the AI industry has invested so heavily in ever-larger models and datasets: research has shown fairly consistent, predictable returns from scaling up these three factors, at least up to a point. Understanding scaling laws helps explain why frontier AI labs are racing to build bigger data centers and why some analysts debate whether those returns are starting to diminish.

short_definition: The degree to which a person can understand how and why an AI model arrived at a particular output.
long_definition: Interpretability is the underlying property; Explainable AI (XAI) refers to the techniques used to improve or surface it. A highly interpretable model's reasoning can be followed step by step; a low-interpretability model (like most large neural networks) functions more like a 'black box,' producing outputs whose internal reasoning is difficult for even its own creators to fully trace.

short_definition: The principle that an AI system should produce equitable outcomes for all individuals and groups, regardless of attributes like race, gender, or age.
long_definition: Fairness is one of the most concrete, practical dimensions of AI ethics: it involves testing whether a model's outputs or decisions disproportionately favor or disadvantage particular groups, and taking steps to correct that when found. It's especially critical in sensitive use cases like hiring, lending, and healthcare, where biased outcomes can cause real harm and carry legal risk.

short_definition: The practical ability to work effectively and responsibly with AI tools - understanding their capabilities, limitations, and appropriate use.
long_definition: AI fluency is less about deep technical knowledge and more about judgment: knowing what an AI tool is good at, when to trust its output and when to double-check it, and how to get useful results out of it. It's essentially the skill this glossary itself is meant to help build.

short_definition: Standardized tests used to measure and compare how well different AI models perform on specific tasks.
long_definition: Benchmarks let researchers and companies compare models on a level playing field - testing how well different models answer questions, solve math problems, or write code. Benchmarks have real limitations (models can be specifically tuned to score well on popular benchmarks without necessarily being better in messier real-world use), so benchmark results are a useful data point, not the whole picture, when choosing a model for a product.

short_definition: New, unexpected abilities that appear in an AI model as it scales up, without being explicitly designed or trained for.
long_definition: As language models have grown larger, they've sometimes displayed capabilities - like basic arithmetic or writing working code - that weren't specifically targeted during training and weren't present in smaller versions of the same model family. Emergent behavior is part of why scaling has been such a major focus in AI research, though it also makes model behavior harder to fully predict in advance.

short_definition: The most advanced AI models available at any given time, representing the current cutting edge of the field.
long_definition: 'Frontier' is a relative, moving target - today's frontier model will be a mid-tier or legacy model within a year or two, as the field advances quickly. The term is commonly used in industry and policy conversations about the most capable (and potentially highest-risk) systems being developed by leading AI labs.

short_definition: Datasets so large or complex that traditional data-processing tools and methods can't handle them effectively.
long_definition: Big data predates the current AI wave by over a decade, but the two are closely linked: the massive datasets that fall under 'big data' are exactly what's needed to train modern machine learning and AI models. It's often described by its volume, velocity (how fast it's generated), and variety (how many different formats/sources it comes from).

short_definition: An AI approach that represents knowledge using explicit symbols, rules, and logic, rather than learning patterns from data.
long_definition: Symbolic AI was the dominant paradigm in early AI research and underlies expert systems - a human encodes structured knowledge and logical rules, and the system reasons over them. It offers strong transparency and explainability but doesn't scale well to messy, ambiguous real-world data the way modern machine learning does. Many current 'Hybrid AI' approaches try to combine the best of both.

short_definition: An approach that combines rule-based symbolic reasoning with data-driven machine learning, aiming to get the benefits of both.
long_definition: Hybrid AI tries to pair the transparency and reliability of explicit rules (Symbolic AI) with the flexibility and pattern-recognition strength of machine learning. This combination can be especially valuable in domains like healthcare or finance, where both explainability and adaptability to complex data genuinely matter.

short_definition: AI approaches that rely on large-scale data and statistical techniques to find patterns, rather than following pre-defined rules.
long_definition: This is effectively the framing term for 'modern AI' as contrasted with older, rule-based (symbolic) approaches - it covers the machine learning and deep learning techniques that power most of today's AI products. It's a useful contrast term mainly in academic or historical discussions of how AI has evolved.

short_definition: An adaptation of the Transformer architecture, originally built for language, applied to image-processing tasks.
long_definition: Vision Transformers process an image by splitting it into small patches and applying the same attention mechanism used in language models, rather than the sliding-filter approach traditional CNNs use. This has allowed some of the same architectural advances driving progress in LLMs to carry over into computer vision.

short_definition: An AI model, developed by OpenAI, that learns to connect images and their text descriptions.
long_definition: CLIP was trained on a huge number of image-caption pairs, learning to recognize which pieces of text describe which images. This connection between vision and language underlies many multimodal AI capabilities, including some image-generation and image-search systems.

short_definition: A machine learning approach where a model keeps learning from new data over time without forgetting what it learned before.
long_definition: Most deployed AI models are effectively frozen after training - they don't keep learning from new interactions. Continual (or 'lifelong') learning is an active research area aiming to let models update incrementally without the common failure mode of 'catastrophic forgetting,' where learning something new erases previously learned knowledge.

short_definition: The general term for whatever goal a model is trying to optimize during training, whether that means minimizing error or maximizing some measure of success.
long_definition: An objective function is the broader concept; a Loss Function is the most common specific case, where the goal is to minimize error. In other contexts, like reinforcement learning, the objective function might instead be something to maximize (like cumulative reward) rather than minimize.

short_definition: An optimization method that gradually adjusts a model's internal values to reduce its errors, step by step.
long_definition: Gradient descent is the mathematical technique behind how a model actually learns from its loss function score: it calculates which direction to nudge each weight to reduce error, then takes a small step in that direction, repeating many times over the course of training.

short_definition: A technique used during training to prevent a model from overfitting by discouraging it from relying too heavily on overly complex patterns.
long_definition: Regularization adds a penalty to the training process that pushes the model toward simpler, more generalizable patterns rather than ones that fit the training data too precisely. It's one of several standard tools (alongside data augmentation and more training data) used to keep a model's performance robust on new, unseen data.

short_definition: A type of neural network that learns to compress data down to its essential features, then reconstruct the original from that compressed form.
long_definition: Autoencoders consist of an encoder (which compresses the input) and a decoder (which reconstructs it), trained by trying to make the output match the input as closely as possible after passing through that compression bottleneck. They're used for tasks like anomaly detection, noise removal, and as a building block within some generative AI systems.

short_definition: A container for numbers organized across multiple dimensions - the basic data structure AI models compute with.
long_definition: A tensor is essentially a generalized version of a spreadsheet: a single number is a 0-dimensional tensor, a list of numbers is 1-dimensional, a grid is 2-dimensional, and so on into higher dimensions used to represent things like batches of images or video.

short_definition: A specialized computer chip designed by Google specifically to accelerate machine learning workloads.
long_definition: TPUs are purpose-built for the kind of matrix and tensor math that neural networks rely on, similar in purpose to GPUs but designed from the ground up for AI rather than adapted from graphics rendering. Google uses TPUs extensively for training and running its own AI models, including Gemini.

short_definition: A simple machine learning method that classifies or predicts a new data point based on the most similar examples already seen.
long_definition: k-NN works by comparing a new item to the 'k' most similar items in the training data and using their characteristics to make a prediction - for example, predicting a house's value based on the sale prices of the most similar nearby houses. It's valued for being simple and easy to understand, though it can be slow on very large datasets.

short_definition: Graphical models that represent probability-based cause-and-effect relationships between different variables.
long_definition: A Bayesian network maps out how different factors influence each other using probabilities rather than certainties - useful for reasoning under uncertainty, like in medical diagnosis or risk assessment, where you rarely have complete information.

short_definition: A machine learning model that makes predictions by asking a sequence of yes/no questions, branching toward a final answer.
long_definition: Decision trees are prized for being relatively easy to interpret - you can trace the exact sequence of questions that led to a given prediction, unlike a neural network's opaque internal reasoning. They're a common building block of more powerful techniques like Ensemble Methods.

short_definition: Machine learning techniques that combine multiple models together to produce a more accurate result than any single model alone.
long_definition: The idea is similar to asking a group of experts for their opinion rather than just one - combining several 'weak' models (like many decision trees) often produces a stronger, more robust prediction. Common approaches include Boosting (training models sequentially, each correcting the last) and Bagging (training many models independently and averaging their results).

short_definition: Simplifying complex data by reducing the number of variables involved, while preserving the most important information.
long_definition: High-dimensional data (data with many variables) can be difficult and computationally expensive to work with directly. Dimensionality reduction techniques compress that data down to its most essential, informative features - similar in spirit to how embeddings compress meaning into a manageable numerical form.

short_definition: The process of discovering patterns and relationships in large datasets using statistical and machine learning methods.
long_definition: Data mining is closely related to, and predates, much of modern machine learning - it's more focused on discovering interesting patterns and insights within existing data (like purchasing habits or fraud indicators) than on building a model to make ongoing future predictions, though the two overlap significantly in practice.

short_definition: The AI-specific framing of using models to forecast future outcomes, trends, or behaviors.
long_definition: Predictive AI covers the same general territory as Predictive Analytics but emphasizes modern machine learning techniques specifically. It's used across functions like risk assessment, resource planning, and demand forecasting, and is often the least flashy but most immediately monetizable category of AI investment for many businesses.

short_definition: The process of extracting meaning from language by examining relationships between words and phrases, not just their literal text.
long_definition: Semantic analysis is what allows a system to understand that 'the bank of the river' and 'money in the bank' use the word 'bank' completely differently, based on context. It's a foundational NLP capability underlying tasks like search, translation, and sentiment analysis.

short_definition: Search that matches results based on meaning and intent, rather than just matching the exact keywords typed in.
long_definition: Traditional keyword search looks for literal word matches; semantic search uses techniques like embeddings to understand that a search for 'affordable family cars' should also surface results about 'budget-friendly minivans,' even without shared keywords. This is core technology behind modern AI-powered search products and RAG systems.

short_definition: An AI system's ability to understand and reason about physical space - how objects relate to, move, and interact with each other in the real world.
long_definition: Spatial intelligence is an emerging frontier for AI research, extending beyond language and 2D image understanding toward genuine 3D physical reasoning - relevant to robotics, autonomous vehicles, and any application where an AI needs to understand real-world physical layouts and movement, not just describe them in words.

short_definition: The general process of adjusting a model's settings to improve its performance on a given goal.
long_definition: Optimization is the umbrella term for the family of techniques (like gradient descent) used to tune a model's parameters so it makes fewer errors or better achieves its objective. It's a foundational concept across virtually every stage of building and training a machine learning model.

short_definition: AI systems designed so their processes and decisions can be reviewed, verified, and traced by humans after the fact.
long_definition: Auditable AI typically involves maintaining detailed logs and documentation of a system's decisions and the data/reasoning behind them, so that outcomes can be reviewed later - important for regulatory compliance and for building trust in sensitive applications like finance or healthcare.

short_definition: The end-to-end process of building, deploying, and maintaining an AI system, from data collection through ongoing monitoring.
long_definition: An AI workflow typically includes stages like data preparation, model training or selection, testing, deployment, and ongoing monitoring for issues like model drift. Understanding this full lifecycle - not just the moment a feature launches - is important for scoping AI work, since maintenance and monitoring are often underestimated costs.

short_definition: The set of practices for reliably deploying, monitoring, and maintaining machine learning models in production.
long_definition: MLOps borrows from software engineering's DevOps discipline, adapting it to the specific challenges of ML - like tracking which data and model version produced which results, detecting when a model's performance degrades, and safely rolling out model updates.

short_definition: MLOps practices adapted specifically for managing large language model applications in production.
long_definition: LLMOps covers concerns specific to LLM-based products - managing prompt versions, tracking token costs, evaluating output quality at scale, and handling the added unpredictability of generative outputs compared to traditional predictive models.

short_definition: An approach to building AI that prioritizes human needs, values, and well-being throughout the design and development process.
long_definition: Human-centered AI treats usability, trust, and real human impact as first-class design considerations, not afterthoughts bolted on after a model is built. It's more a design philosophy and set of priorities than a specific technique, and it overlaps significantly with Responsible AI practice.

short_definition: Low-quality AI-generated content - text, images, or video - produced in high volume with little effort or editorial oversight.
long_definition: 'Slop' has become common shorthand for the flood of low-effort AI content saturating search results and social media, often produced purely to capture ad revenue or views. It's a useful term to know both as an industry/culture reference point and as a cautionary example of what to avoid when designing AI-assisted content features.

short_definition: A general term for large-scale AI models with billions or more parameters, trained on vast, diverse datasets.
long_definition: 'Large Models' overlaps heavily with Foundation Model - both describe massive, broadly-capable systems like GPT or Gemini. The main nuance is that 'foundation model' more often emphasizes being a base that other applications get built on top of, while 'large model' is more simply a description of scale.

short_definition: Running many computations at the same time rather than one after another, to get work done faster.
long_definition: Parallelization is fundamental to how modern AI is trained and run: GPUs are specifically designed to perform thousands of calculations simultaneously, which is a big part of why they became the standard hardware for AI. Better parallelization strategies across many chips and machines have become an important factor in how quickly and affordably new models can be built.

short_definition: A measure of how many tokens an AI system can process or generate in a given amount of time.
long_definition: Token throughput reflects how much AI work a system can handle at once - a key metric for AI infrastructure teams, since it determines how many users a model can serve simultaneously and how quickly each one gets a response.

short_definition: The time it takes an AI model to produce the very first piece of its response after receiving a prompt.
long_definition: TTFT matters especially for real-time, conversational products - even if a full response takes a while to finish generating, a fast TTFT makes an interaction feel responsive because the user sees something happening quickly.

short_definition: A separate portion of data, held back from training, used to check how well a model is learning during development.
long_definition: Validation data lets engineers tune a model's settings (hyperparameters) and catch problems like overfitting before the model is tested against a final, completely untouched test set. It's distinct from both training data (used to teach the model) and test data (used for a final, unbiased performance check).

short_definition: A running measure of how well a model is performing on validation data during training - lower is generally better.
long_definition: Researchers track validation loss closely during training as a kind of real-time progress report: if it stops improving or starts getting worse while training loss keeps improving, that's a warning sign of overfitting. It's commonly used to decide when to stop training a model.

short_definition: Anthropic's framework describing the core goals for how Claude should behave: being useful, truthful, and safe.
long_definition: HHH is a specific, named example of an AI alignment framework - a helpful AI tries to genuinely assist with the task at hand, an honest one avoids hallucinating or overstating its certainty, and a harmless one declines requests that could cause harm and explains why. It's a good concrete illustration of what 'alignment' looks like in practice for a real, deployed product.

short_definition: AI systems designed to maintain performance and efficiency as data volume, task complexity, or user demand grows.
